item.content:encoded:
“Kickers are too good now” sounds plausible when long field goals keep making the highlights. But in the November 9 episode of The Monday Morning Agent, our AI analyst found that long kicks went through at roughly the same rate across the seasons on file. Coaches were attempting them more often. We gave the agent written visualization standards so its charts would show both success rates and attempts per game, with the context readers need to judge the claim.

Decide how to draw the trend before seeing the answer

We started with two charts of league-wide field goal success rates. One began in 2024, with a vertical axis starting around 84%. The line climbed to 85.6%, and the improvement looked dramatic.

The other included every season from 2021 onward, started the vertical axis at zero, and showed the attempt count beneath each point. Success rates stayed around 84% to 86%. The recent rise looked much smaller in that context.

Changing the starting year and axis made the recent improvement look larger. Before your agent draws a trend, decide which choices it can make. Otherwise, it can produce a persuasive picture without giving readers the context to assess it.

Keep the definitions when you add a new capability

The dictionary from episode two still applies. During a rehearsal, that earlier agent refused the kicking claim because its dictionary could describe a rush but couldn’t describe a kick. We expanded what it could define while keeping the requirement to use a saved definition.

This time, the play descriptions named field goals and included distances. We still had to decide where “long” starts. A recognizable play name doesn’t settle how to group it for analysis.

We examined distance bands separately. Kickers made roughly 95% of attempts under 40 yards. Success rates hovered around 80% for attempts from 40 to 49 yards and around 70% for those from 50 to 59 yards. Combining them into one rate can hide the differences the question asks about.

Make the chart standard specific enough to enforce

We introduced eight rules. Every trend includes all seasons on file, and axes start at zero. Each point shows its underlying count. Yellow identifies the subject of the claim, blue identifies the comparison, and gray marks the current season.

The chart title asks a question rather than announcing a conclusion. A source line gives the exact command that produced the data, so readers can rerun it. The chart shows only values the tool printed, without added trend lines or numbers typed by hand. Every chart uses the same layout, with success rates above attempts per game.

Writing these standards down gives the agent consistent instructions and gives readers a familiar way to compare results across episodes. Choose standards that fit your analysis, then specify how you’ll check each one.

Test a chart that breaks the rules

A written standard needs a way to enforce it. We added a renderer, the program that turns the agent’s chart specification into a picture. It checks the chart specification against the rules before drawing the chart and refuses specifications that break them.

We deliberately requested a trend beginning in 2023. The renderer refused because the first season on file was 2021. Its response identified the rule instead of producing the shortened chart.

Give your agent a request that violates a standard and inspect the response. That check shows whether the restriction works when the agent tries to produce an output.

Show how much evidence sits behind each rate

The longest kicks need particular care. The episode’s current-season sample contained only nine attempts in the group of kicks from 60 yards or farther. The next kick could noticeably change that rate. Displaying counts beside percentages helps readers distinguish a small sample from hundreds of attempts.

Showing success rates alongside attempts per game helped explain the ruling. In these plays, long kicks weren’t consistently becoming more successful; coaches were trying them more often. More attempts give fans more opportunities to see a long field goal go through.

We also corrected episode two’s results after finding an error in the tool. Our defined substitute for the tush push had a conversion advantage of 10.1 percentage points overall and 9.7 without Philadelphia, replacing the previously reported 8.3 and 7.8. Chart standards help readers inspect results, but we still have to check the calculations behind them.

Next up: “The Pundit Audit”

On November 16, we’ll add a second agent to independently audit an audience-selected claim. We’ll examine where the agents disagree and how they investigate the evidence. The agent doing the analysis shouldn’t also grade its own work.

O’Reilly members can sign up on the O’Reilly learning platform to join us live on November 23, 8:00am–8:45am PT / 11:00am–11:45am ET. Everyone can follow along on Radar every other Monday, with a brief pause for the holidays. Watch episode three above, and we’ll build on it in the next session.

item.title: When AI Can Code, What Is Left for Programmers to Do?
item.dc:creator: Shahid N. Shah and Andy Oram
item.description: AI is in such widespread use for programming that project maintainers (particularly for free and open source software) are complaining about the burden of reviewing mounds of low-quality code. In fact, AI can help with every stage of code development: writing the specification, coding, uncovering bugs, and repairing the code. This article describes human-AI collaboration […]
item.content:encoded:
AI is in such widespread use for programming that project maintainers (particularly for free and open source software) are complaining about the burden of reviewing mounds of low-quality code. In fact, AI can help with every stage of code development: writing the specification, coding, uncovering bugs, and repairing the code. This article describes human-AI collaboration at specification and code repair stages, and lays out the skills that humans need to accomplish those tasks in the current generation of AI. We won’t cover coding and bug finding because they are widely discussed elsewhere.

Let the AI harness write the spec

We don’t want developers hand-writing specs. We want them in a room, or on a call, talking with the product manager (PM) and the customer.

Humans reach a limit when writing. We skip the boring cases. We get tired by requirement 40. We use “customer” on page 1 and “client” on page 6 of the spec. We write down what we remember and forget what we assumed. AI has the patience and diligence we lack.

It’s still up to human developers to write guardrails or constraints into the spec: statements to ensure that nothing wildly wrong makes it into code. Each guardrail should be one sentence that says MUST or MUST NOT, with a proof beside it: a test, a check, or a named person who reviews it. A guardrail with no proof is a wish. Write the guardrails first, because the PM won’t think of most of them. What must never happen? Who must never see this? What should the agent never touch?

With guardrails in place, capture the conversation and let the machine do the writing. Two AI tools have shown themselves particularly useful to analyze requirements: The Plaud Note recorder attaches to the back of your phone and records in-person conversations and phone calls; the wearable NotePin records in-person conversations, not phone calls. Granola runs on your laptop or phone, uses your computer’s audio, and analyzes what it captures. We find these products to be a leap above common AI tools for summarizing conversations, when it comes to specification development.

Plaud and Granola (if you prompt them to do so) can notice what’s missing and tell you the gaps in the requirements. They ask, What happens when this field is empty? What if two people do this at once? Who is allowed to see it? over and over, for every requirement, and check each noun in the requirements against an ontology created by the programmer (often with the help of AI).

The developer, the PM, and the customer read the output from the AI, fix what’s wrong, answer what’s missing, and go through the process again.

The spec that comes out of that loop tends to be more complete and more consistent than what the same people write alone. That’s Shahid’s own experience, not a study, but it matches reports from some other people at the leading edge of the use of AI for software development. Mark Pike, a product lawyer at Anthropic, builds working tools for his legal team without writing code: “I just typed a normal sentence, describing what I wanted. And it worked.” StrongDM, which runs a software factory where agents write and test the code, says the starting point for a piece of software can be “a few sentences, a screenshot, or an existing codebase.”

Keep the spec after the feature ships. As you prepare a new version of the product next year, it can tell you why the code looks the way it does.

The data schema is the other half of the spec

Most teams treat the data schema as plumbing. Tables get named by whoever got there first. The spec, reflecting human conversation, may say customer, account, client, and org at different places for the same thing, and you have to choose one noun for the schema. A human learns the mapping by sitting next to the person who wrote it. An AI agent has no neighbor to consult, so it guesses—with results that likely differ from Monday to Tuesday.

So the developer must keep an ontology, which here means a written, machine-checkable account of the things the program manipulates, how they relate, and who may see them. For example, in an appointment scheduling application, the ontology might define a Patient, Doctor, Appointment, and Time Slot. It would specify that a Patient can book multiple Appointments, each Appointment must have exactly one Doctor, a Doctor cannot have two Appointments in the same Time Slot, and only authorized people can view or change an Appointment. These aren’t just database tables or fields. They’re the business concepts, relationships, and rules that give the data meaning.

Creating this ontology requires developers to identify terms, resolve ambiguities, and agree on rules that everyone might otherwise assume are obvious. It’s rigorous, sometimes tedious work, but it’s an essential human responsibility. The ontology connects what the business wants (requirements), how the software should behave (specification), and how information is stored (schema). It also gives AI coding agents a precise definition of what they’re building instead of leaving them to guess.

The ontology doesn’t have to be a university project. Start with twenty terms that AI can help you generate from your specs. Every noun in a spec maps to a type. Every type points back to the spec that justifies it. If either side is orphaned, a check fails. Every record says who may see it from day one, and when it doesn’t, the spec defaults to the most restrictive audience.

Use standard vocabularies like the ones at schema.org before you invent your own. A frontier AI model has read far more about schema.org than about your private names, so a standard term brings its meaning along. We expect that to make the schema more useful, though we haven’t tested that hypothesis. Your name for an invoice isn’t a feature, so you don’t have to be creative about it.

As customer requirements change, the developers must change the ontology to keep up.

So the process, in a nutshell, is to develop the spec by using AI on customer-stated requirements. Then a human develops the ontology (often in collaboration with AI too), which is used to create a consistent schema. Finally, create and test the code. Teams that go the other way end up with an agent writing against a poorly defined vocabulary, setting up the reviewer to spend an afternoon or even a week figuring out what it meant.

Ontologies might help avoid a reciprocal problem: different parts of an organization assigning different meanings to the same term.

We’ll admit we can’t prove you need all this. Anthropic had sixteen agents write a C compiler, and the researcher said the verifier had to be nearly perfect. He used GCC as a known-good reference. A compiler has that reference. Most companies don’t. Nobody has a GCC for “may this customer see this document” or “can this contract move to the next stage.” Our bet is that the spec and the schema are your test suite for that kind of question.

Now on to bug fixing.

Don’t clean up after the AI. Build the tool that does.

An agent can hand you a 3,000-line pull request before lunch. With AI coding, reviewing has suddenly become much more expensive than writing. When a person is the first line of defense, that person turns into the bottleneck and then starts skimming, which is almost as bad as no review at all.

The usual advice is to review harder. We’d rather that a person reads very little, and that what they do read is worth the time. For example, reading the specs, reading test harnesses to validate the spec and refining the ontology is worth it, but reviewing generated code which passes the tests is probably not. Developers promise they’ll tidy up the AI’s mess as it comes. Don’t.

The OpenAI team that built a product with no handwritten code tried it. They spent every Friday, a fifth of the week, cleaning up what they called “AI slop.” It didn’t last. So they wrote their guardrails down as “golden principles,” set up an agent that scans for stale documentation and opens fix-up pull requests, and wrote their lint messages “to inject remediation instructions into agent context.” A living check doesn’t just fail on buggy code. It tells the agent how to fix the problem.

The harness we’d build first consists of:

  • A command line that’s built deterministically, without calling upon AI, to make sure that the highest level of the process can’t take off in an unanticipated direction.
  • A gate before code. If a change touches code and nothing in the specs or the schema changed, stop and ask why.
  • A second pass. Here, anything generated gets rebuilt from scratch and compared to what’s committed. If Git identifies differences that should not be there, that can be an important review finding and it deserves changing a guardrail, not handwriting new code.
  • A weekly drift audit. It lists specs that cite requirements that don’t exist, requirements with no proof, schema terms used nowhere, and tests that name no requirement. It flags what’s suspicious and offers solutions. It’s read-only; a person makes the choices and resolves what to do.
  • A route from every catch to a permanent check. Sierra, which builds customer service agents, has experts annotate sampled conversations, and those “become the basis for the agent’s regression tests.” A harness should upgrade its coding so that each bug happens only once, and can be avoided by the harness in the future.
  • Limits on what agents may do. Some actions they take themselves, whereas others they only propose. Some belong to a named person who signs with a reason. An agent that wants a decision writes a proposal.

StrongDM found out why the last two bullet items matter. Their agents learned that return true is “a great way to pass narrowly written tests,” so they use end-to-end “scenarios,” often stored outside the codebase, as holdout tests that the coding agent cannot see. The principle is the same as investigating ethics violations at an agency: We’d want the investigation conducted by someone outside the agency.

We should say where Shahid’s present harness falls short. As far as we know, nothing yet checks whether names in the requirement exist also in the spec. Furthermore, the project runs no continuous integration service and no automatic hooks, so running the checks is a habit instead of a rule. Those are the next things they will build, and building them is humans’ work.

With the technique described here, the review burden that used to be spiraling out of control actually shrinks. A person reads a short spec with a proof on every line, and the machine checks the rest.

Put three new lines in developers’ job descriptions

We suggest that next Monday you try changing job descriptions to reflect the tasks stated at the beginning of this article. Tell each developer:

  1. You hold the conversation with the PM and the customer, and the harness drafts the spec and the guardrails from it. A spec isn’t done until every requirement has a proof.
  2. You own the ontology. A word in a spec that isn’t in the final schema reveals a bug.
  3. You build the harness that audits and repairs the repository. If you’re cleaning the code by hand, the harness is missing something.

Try the process on one feature. Ask permission before recording a conversation. Plaud’s own guidance is to give people a quick heads-up while noting that local regulations differ. Granola has written about how to tell the people it’s transcribing. Customers who know you’re recording them in order to get their requirements right usually don’t mind.

Let the harness draft the spec. Read its list of gaps. Check every noun against the ontology. Add a check that would have caught the most recent bug you fixed by hand. If your reviews get shorter and your bug count stays flat, keep going.

What this process is and is not

This article grows from Shahid’s experience and represents our opinions, and we can’t point to a controlled study. But controlled studies are similarly lacking for nearly all the advice programmers and software architects have gotten over the decades. (Check out the O’Reilly book Making Software for a discussion of rigorous research in software.) We can cite companies that believe they’re more productive and more responsive to their customers by following roughly the process outlined in this article.

Some people who look at the three job descriptions we’ve listed think we’re turning developers into paper pushers. We think the reverse. The programmers are responsible for high-level tasks that do not fall into the old categories of architecture, coding, and testing. Our bet is that you and every developer you know will be doing something like this within a couple years.

item.title: This Week in AI: Who Gets to Benefit from AI?
item.dc:creator: Christina Stathopoulos and Michelle Smith
item.custom:subtitle: Frontier models, regional AI, and responsible development
item.description: AI is becoming more capable at handling everyday tasks, but benefiting from that progress depends increasingly on where people live, what language they speak, and how much control they have over the technology. On the latest episode of This Week in AI, we examined developments from OpenAI and Anthropic, the growing push for regional AI […]
item.content:encoded:
AI is becoming more capable at handling everyday tasks, but benefiting from that progress depends increasingly on where people live, what language they speak, and how much control they have over the technology. On the latest episode of This Week in AI, we examined developments from OpenAI and Anthropic, the growing push for regional AI models, and the challenges of making AI more accessible and responsible.

Frontier AI is moving into everyday services

OpenAI introduced LifeVal, a benchmark that measures how well AI handles everyday tasks such as finding childcare, managing household budgets, and accessing government services. Scores rose from 49% for GPT-5.2 to roughly 80% for GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra. This could help researchers assess whether improvements in model capabilities translate into useful assistance with daily responsibilities.

OpenAI reported that ChatGPT now handles roughly 20% of Google’s search volume in search-like queries, although the company hasn’t explained its methodology. Its new GPT-6 Cyber model, available to approved security teams, aims to help identify and fix software vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, Anthropic began testing read-only banking connections in Claude, allowing some US subscribers to analyze spending and identify unusual charges. As AI assistants take on tasks traditionally handled by banks, search engines, and specialized software, those industries will have to reconsider how they serve customers and protect their data.

Anthropic also published FlashProve, a research prototype that uses cryptographic proofs to verify which model generated a response. Separately, nonprofit research organization METR reported that AI assistance may have roughly doubled the pace of progress on certain model development tasks at Anthropic over the past year. The findings don’t establish recursive self-improvement, but they suggest that AI assistance is already speeding up parts of model development. That makes it increasingly important to understand how AI is shaping that progress and to check the reliability of the outputs these systems produce.

Regional AI addresses gaps in access

We’ve previously discussed the “tokenizer tax,” which makes some languages more expensive to process because they require more tokens than English. New research from the University of Michigan found another disadvantage. In one test, answering questions in Pashto consumed up to 179 times more energy than answering equivalent questions in English, while accuracy also suffered. The findings show how language can affect both the cost and quality of AI services.

Countries are responding by investing in models designed around their own languages and infrastructure. Ibero-American countries agreed to form a regional AI alliance to coordinate model development, data sharing, and computing resources. India introduced three domestic models, including EKA-1, which supports 22 Indian languages and English, and two Dhīr models designed to work offline with documents. Offline capabilities could make these systems especially useful in rural areas with unreliable internet access.

Indonesia’s GoTo, the UAE’s Jais 3, and Uganda’s Sunflower V2 are further examples of projects developing AI for local languages. These efforts could give developers more control over AI for local languages and reduce reliance on proprietary AI services, even when some build on open foundation models from larger labs. They could also make AI more useful in languages that existing models handle poorly. For organizations deploying AI across multiple countries, testing performance and cost in each language may reveal problems that English-language benchmarks miss.

Responsible AI depends on how we deploy it

Google faced criticism over changes to AI controls in school accounts. Under a new arrangement, schools that disable AI also lose access to Google Search. That leaves educators with limited control over which tools students can use. And in Europe, an advisor to the EU’s top court suggested that chatbots could infringe publishers’ rights when reproducing news content. The opinion emerged from a dispute involving Google’s Gemini and a Hungarian publisher. A final ruling is still pending, but the case could influence how AI companies access and reuse copyrighted material. This is part of a broader wave of publisher lawsuits, including The New York Times’ US case against OpenAI and Microsoft over the alleged use of its articles to train models and reproduce content in ChatGPT outputs.

AI’s environmental costs continue to come into focus. Some data center operators are repurposing retired jet engines as natural gas generators to obtain power while waiting for grid connections. Although this can accelerate deployment, the converted engines are less efficient and can produce more pollution than conventional turbines, meaning faster access to electricity comes at the expense of higher emissions and worse local air quality. Public opposition is growing too. During the November 3 US general elections, voters favored restrictions on data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states.

Meanwhile, Planet introduced a natural-language tool for searching and analyzing more than a decade of satellite imagery. Users can explore geographic changes without specialized GIS expertise, making satellite data easier for people without that background to investigate. The application shows how AI can help more people work with complex data that previously required specialized tools and training.

What’s next

As AI expands into personal services and countries invest in their own models, developers and organizations face increasingly different requirements for security, performance, and accessibility. The most useful systems will be those that work reliably for the people and circumstances they’re designed to serve.

We’ll be back on Monday, November 16, for another episode covering the latest developments in AI research and applications. You can catch previous episodes on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.title: What Makes an Agent Self-Evolving?
item.dc:creator: Annie Wang
item.description: An agent can get better at its job without a new model. It can learn to find useful information, choose the right tool, or check that a task is finished before reporting success. For that experience to help with the next task, something has to carry over: an updated instruction, a lesson saved in memory, […]
item.content:encoded:
An agent can get better at its job without a new model. It can learn to find useful information, choose the right tool, or check that a task is finished before reporting success. For that experience to help with the next task, something has to carry over: an updated instruction, a lesson saved in memory, or a change to the software that runs the agent.

That is what interests me about a self-evolving agent: It can use experience to change how it handles future tasks. Much of that change happens in the harness, the instructions, context, tools, and software around the model. Research such as Harness-RSI explores how agents can change that harness while continuing to use the same model.

Of course, a change can make things worse. A saved memory might be wrong, or a new instruction might fix one problem and create another. I think about self-evolving agents in three parts: evaluation to tell whether a change helped, an improvement process that can do more of the work on its own, and the parts of the harness it is allowed to change.

Evaluation: What counts as improvement?

Before I ask an agent to improve itself, I want to know what doing a better job would look like. A model’s score on a benchmark tells us how it performed on that test. To evaluate an agent built with that model, we also need to ask whether it used the right information, took the right actions, and met the user’s requirements.

In a restaurant-planning exercise I developed for teaching evaluation, an agent is given a group’s needs and information about restaurants. Its job is to suggest a place and a time for dinner. The people and restaurants are fictional, but success is easy to understand: Can everyone eat there, afford it, and make it on time?

In one test, the agent recommended a restaurant that met everyone’s needs. My evaluation still marked the answer as wrong because it compared the wording with a sample answer I had written. But my answer was only one possible solution. A different recommendation could work just as well. That feedback could lead a self-improving agent to “fix” a decision that was already good.

A more useful evaluation would check whether the recommendation met the group’s requirements. If someone’s budget is $25 and the meal costs $28, the plan fails that check. We can build a custom evaluation around those requirements, checking the price, dietary needs, and timing. Other questions require judgment, such as whether the agent clearly explained a trade-off between price and convenience. A person or another model can help assess those.

If we asked the agent to make a booking as well, we would need to check that the reservation actually existed. A message saying, “Your table is booked” would not be enough. Evaluating the system means checking what it did, as well as what it said.

Once the agent proposes a change, we can test the updated version against the current one. It should still handle tasks it already did well. We should also try cases that were not used to develop or choose the change. Getting one dinner plan right tells us less than handling new groups with different budgets, dietary needs, and schedules.

The evaluation should also explain why an answer failed. “The meal costs more than the guest’s budget” gives the agent something specific to investigate. It still needs to find the cause, but it knows where to start.

Autonomous improvement: Who carries the work forward?

If an engineer has to spot every failure, suggest every change, and start every test, improvement still depends on that person. Autonomous improvement means giving more of this work to the system. It can review past tasks, look for repeated mistakes, propose a change, and test whether the change helps.

For example, a more autonomous dinner planner might notice that it repeatedly recommended restaurants people could not afford, even though their budgets were available. It could try a new instruction: remove restaurants that exceed anyone’s budget before comparing the remaining options. It would then test that instruction on other groups. If the results improve and the agent still handles tasks it previously got right, it can keep the change. Otherwise, it keeps the current version.

There are two kinds of work here. While planning a dinner, the agent uses tools, reads the results, and decides what to do next. That is its task loop. The improvement process looks back across those attempts and changes how it will approach future tasks. An agent can plan dinner on its own and still depend on an engineer to teach it a better way to plan.

This review does not have to happen after every request. The system might start it after several similar failures, or review a day’s work overnight. Looking at several tasks together helps it see which problems keep coming back.

We can give the system more responsibility gradually. At first, it might investigate problems and test changes, then ask an engineer to approve them. Later, it might also keep certain kinds of changes on its own. The team still decides what it may change, how much time or money it may spend experimenting, and when a person needs to step in.

Harness modules: What can evolve?

When an agent makes a poor decision, I want to find the cause before rewriting its instructions. If a guest’s budget never reached the model, telling it to “pay attention to the budget” will not help. We need to fix how that information reaches the model.

ModularRSI divides the harness into five parts: context management, the agent loop, tool use, observation management, and task completion detection. It studies changes to these parts separately before putting them together. This gives us a useful way to ask what exactly an agent could improve.

Context management comes first for me. It determines what information the model has when it makes a decision, including which memories are brought into the current task. Reflective memory means looking back at what happened and saving a lesson that could help next time. For the dinner planner, that lesson might be to check everyone’s budget and dietary needs before comparing restaurants.

The memory needs to distinguish a general lesson from a fact about one person. “Check the budget before recommending a restaurant” could help with any group. “This guest has a $25 budget” applies to a particular person and occasion. Without that context, the agent could use an old fact in the wrong situation.

Dreaming is a way to review and organize memories between sessions. The system goes back over past interactions and what it has already stored, combines related observations, and saves useful lessons. When memories disagree, it needs to check the original evidence before deciding what to keep. Anthropic’s Dreams, for example, produces a reorganized set of memories that can be reviewed before later sessions use them.

What I want from dreaming is a better starting point for the next task. The agent should be able to find a useful lesson without reading every previous conversation again. We can test that by comparing how it handles new tasks with the old and revised memories. Organizing memories overnight only counts as an improvement if the results support that claim.

The agent could also improve how it finds and organizes memories. Saving one lesson may help with a future task. Changing the way it selects lessons could help it make better use of many future experiences.

The other four modules affect how the agent does its work:

  • Agent loop: The agent plans, acts, and decides what to do next. It could learn to notice when it is repeating an unsuccessful approach and try a different one.
  • Tool use: Tools the agent has and how it uses them. It could add a tool it needs or change a tool’s interface to make it easier to use correctly.
  • Observation management: The agent handles the information returned by its tools. It could change how it summarizes a result so that an important fact is not lost.
  • Task completion detection: The agent decides that the job is done. It could check for confirmation that an action succeeded before telling the user it is finished.

These parts work together. Changing a tool can change the information the agent receives, which can change its next decision. Testing one module helps us understand a change. Testing the whole agent tells us whether the parts still work well together.

Improvement becomes recursive when the agent uses its updated harness to carry out the next round of improvement. Suppose it changes how it searches past runs for examples of a failure. The next time it tries to improve itself, it uses that new search method to decide what to investigate and test. A change made in one round now shapes how it works on the next one.

This gives the agent a chance to get better at finding and testing improvements, as well as doing its original job. Each round builds on changes that were kept from earlier rounds. To find out whether that helps, we need to check whether later rounds produce changes that work better on new tasks.

I want an agent that needs less repeated correction because it has learned a better way to do the job. We should be able to point to what it learned, what changed, and how we checked that the change helped. Then we can see whether that lesson holds up when the agent has a new task to do.

item.dc:creator: Ben Lorica and Duncan Davidson

item.content:encoded:
This post was created with the assistance of AI, based on a transcript of the conversation.

AI tools have started to remember their users, but each tool remembers a different version of the same person. Duncan Davidson, an independent consultant and longtime software engineer, has been trying to connect those fragments. He joined Ben Lorica to discuss what personal AI could do if people could carry their context between services and decide what each service gets to see.

They also talked about how AI coding changed web development during Duncan’s time at Webflow, what new developers may lose as entry-level work changes, and why open source projects need new ways to handle AI-assisted contributions.

About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World, Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise.

Check out other episodes of this podcast on the O’Reilly learning platform or follow us on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Takeaways

06.31 The developer’s job is moving toward outcomes. Duncan compared AI coding to desktop publishing, which removed the physical work of assembling pages but left designers responsible for what the page should look like. At Webflow, he saw people use AI tools to make websites faster than they could with earlier tools. For developers, he said, the question has shifted from how quickly they can type code to “What outcome do you want? What are you trying to do with this code, and how can you make it better?” People still need to judge whether an implementation fits the rest of the system.

10.41 New developers still need a way to become experts. Computer science fundamentals still matter when an agent offers several plausible fixes and a person must choose the one that fits a larger system. Ben asked where future engineers will gain that judgment if AI absorbs entry-level tasks. Duncan compared early career work to an apprenticeship in the arts, where even menial assignments expose newcomers to how the whole operation works. Companies that measure only throughput, he warned, may leave too little room for people to learn.

23.07 AI-assisted changes are straining open source review. Duncan described a library he uses in one of his apps. His fixes, along with performance problems Claude noticed, left his version roughly 25 pull requests ahead of the project’s main branch. The maintainers were using AI too, he said. The difficulty was getting useful changes back to the project without overwhelming its review process. His conclusion was that older open source collaboration practices need a “serious retrofit.”

28.27 Personal memory is fragmented across tools. Duncan first had his coding agents save useful information into a collection of Markdown files. Once commercial agents added memory, he found that “Claude knew me one way and ChatGPT knows me another way.” He could push context back to each tool with instructions and occasional reminders, but that solution demands more tinkering than most people want to do. What he wants is a small set of shared mechanisms that let a person carry context across services.

34.01 Portable memory needs boundaries. A prompt’s context, an agent’s memory of recent interactions, and a person’s longer-term knowledge should be able to travel, but Duncan also wants people to control access by scope. He keeps general notes alongside information about his family and finances. His test for a useful system is whether he can say, “Give Claude access to these scopes of my knowledge, but not everything.” That becomes harder when a personal agent encounters knowledge gained at work. Duncan left open where an employee’s own expertise ends and an employer’s information begins.

36.44 Trust and security shape what people will share. Ben’s not yet comfortable letting a consumer agent reach into his finances. Duncan noted that trust would have to grow through experience, as it would with a human agent. We’re already seeing how AI agents can find vulnerabilities faster than established disclosure practices can handle. Duncan expects software maintainers to face more pressure as agents uncover latent bugs, while Ben questioned how quickly organizations that rely on vulnerable code would learn about the findings. People need control over what an agent can access and confidence in the systems around it.

49.52 A personal memory could answer requests with permission. Duncan imagined keeping his memory on his phone and giving a new service a way to request specific information. A car dealership’s agent, for example, could ask for details, but the phone would seek his approval before sharing them. He put it this way:

I could provide it a handle to my memory. And whatever agents they’re working with can come in and ping me and say, “Hey, we’d like to know these things about you.” And it wouldn’t necessarily do it automatically.

item.title: Why Git Needs Help: Moving from Files to Systems for Source Control
item.dc:creator: Jason Davenport
item.description: The shift to agentic reality When Git was designed in 2005, Linus Torvalds solved a brilliant problem for humans collaborating over terminal windows by trading line-by-line diffs. Fast-forward to 2026: Autonomous coding agents don’t think in flat text files or line breaks. They reason across syntax trees, execution traces, call graphs, and type constraints. In […]
item.content:encoded:
The shift to agentic reality

When Git was designed in 2005, Linus Torvalds solved a brilliant problem for humans collaborating over terminal windows by trading line-by-line diffs. Fast-forward to 2026: Autonomous coding agents don’t think in flat text files or line breaks. They reason across syntax trees, execution traces, call graphs, and type constraints. In my view, forcing an AI agent to engineer complex distributed systems through string matching is like handing a chief software architect a chisel and a stack of sticky notes.

File-centric versus system-centric paradigm shift

Whenever I see engineers try to lock context-blind models into file-centric version control, I watch the consequences compound quickly. Context windows fill with irrelevant churn, API bills surge, and subtle, multifile structural breakages slip past basic syntax checks. Just as critically, standard Git discards the cognitive history of a change. The moment an agent session completes, its execution logs, compiler feedback, and discarded hypotheses evaporate into thin air.

Tactical illustration: renaming a distributed method signature

Consider updating a core helper signature across 40 dependent services. A traditional string diff forces the agent to read and mutate thousands of lines of surrounding boilerplate text, burning thousands of context tokens per file:

--- a/services/auth.py
+++ b/services/auth.py
@@ -42,7 +42,7 @@ class AuthManager:
     def validate_session(self, token: str) -> UserSession:
-        return fetch_user_by_token(token)
+        return fetch_user_by_token(token, include_metadata=True)

In contrast, an AST mutation node isolates the target function symbol, executing the change precisely without passing unneeded ambient text through the prompt window:

{
  "action": "mutate_node",
  "target_ast_id": "ast_node_89f2a41b",
  "symbol": "fetch_user_by_token",
  "update": {
    "add_argument": { "name": "include_metadata", "value": true }
  }
}

This exact bottleneck hit Anthropic in late 2026. As autonomous agent activity pushed monorepo merges beyond 30,000 per day, conventional Git infrastructure simply buckled under the load. To me, unlocking genuine agentic autonomy requires evolving source control along two complementary tracks: shifting to server-hosted, graph-aware architectures, and treating agent reasoning as a first-class, versioned artifact right alongside the code itself.

Why text diffs and ephemeral sessions create silent debt

Standard diff tools operate purely on raw Unicode strings. When an agent reorders functions or cleans up formatting, string diffs pollute context windows with noise while remaining blind to structural reality. If you modify a single method signature, Git won’t warn you about the dozen callers broken across separate modules. From my experience, feeding 2,000-line source files into prompts just to update a 5-line helper method degrades model attention, burns compute, and inflates overhead at scale.

Text diffs versus AST graph mutations

Compounding this structural blind spot is what I consider our biggest waste: ephemeral session memory. Whenever an agent finishes a task or compacts its context window, its entire diagnostic history—failed attempts, shell outputs, and compiler warnings—disappears. The next agent assigned to the branch steps in completely blind, doomed to repeat the same diagnostic dead ends and burn unnecessary tokens.

Agent-native architectures in practice

In my view, next-generation version control must replace raw file trees with Tree-sitter parsers and code property graphs (CPGs). Instead of editing lines on disk, agents mutate specific syntax nodes directly, executing sub-second edits and running immediate dependency impact checks across the codebase. Moving control back to the server eliminates the massive I/O bottlenecks caused by checking out heavy working trees onto virtual machines, allowing agents to query and update code over fast graph end points.

Practical implementation: server-side microdiff stream

Below is an example payload representing an atomic microdiff layer executed directly on a server-hosted code property graph, bypassing local file checkouts entirely:

{
  "commit_id": "c_9011f4a2",
  "parent_graph_version": "v14.2.0",
  "operations": [
    {
      "op": "replace_node_property",
      "node_uri": "cpg://auth_service/ast/Node_441",
      "property": "return_type",
      "value": "Promise<UserSession>"
    }
  ],
  "validation_hash": 
  "sha256_e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855"
}

This structural shift pairs naturally with stacked microdiffs—atomic, dependent layers verified sequentially in isolated virtual workspaces to prevent merge races. I was particularly impressed seeing the real-world impact of this pattern with Anthropic’s Scion architecture. Faced with object-store locks and clone latencies as daily merges scaled 10x, Anthropic built a server-centric SCM that streams code graphs on demand, slashing infrastructure overhead by 200x while enabling near-instant workspace initialization.

Versioning reasoning and system memory

I strongly believe code changes alone rarely capture full intent. Modern SCM must link model reasoning traces, prompt chains, and decision graphs directly to commit nodes, preserving architectural context for future debugging and audits. Persisting build outputs, compiler logs, and linter runs in execution ledgers attached to commit trees allows subsequent agents to inspect prior test results instantly rather than rerunning identical test suites.

System memory schema: reasoning and execution ledger

To prevent model sessions from repeating diagnostic dead ends, execution ledgers append structured reasoning and compiler feedback directly to commit nodes:

{
  "agent_session_id": "sess_88190c2a",
  "target_commit": "c_9011f4a2",
  "hypothesis_tree": {
    "attempt_1": { "approach": "In-memory caching", "status": "REJECTED", 
    "reason": "Memory limit exceeded in integration test" },
    "attempt_2": { "approach": "Redis backing store", "status": 
    "VERIFIED", "execution_time_ms": 142 }
  },
  "compiler_ledger": {
    "linter_passed": true,
    "type_check_errors": 0
  }
}

By explicitly recording abandoned branches and failed architectural hypotheses as structured metadata, we stop future agent sessions from reexploring invalid paths. I argue that capturing thought streams alongside code transforms source control from a passive text archive into an active memory system.

The hard engineering trade-offs and counterarguments

I won’t pretend making this transition is easy; it comes with steep engineering trade-offs. Existing developer tooling, from LSPs to build pipelines and IDEs, expects standard local file trees. Replacing checkouts with server-hosted graphs requires building heavy compatibility layers or redesigning workflows. Furthermore, human reviewers still digest code line by line, creating a natural tension with pure graph mutations, while storing continuous thought streams drives up storage and compliance costs. During early refactoring, syntax is often broken and unparseable, forcing systems to temporarily fall back to raw text. Overcoming Git’s decades of deep ecosystem lock-in remains a major operational hurdle we cannot ignore.

Trade-off matrix: architectural migration challenges

Bottom line

Git was designed for humans reviewing text, but agentic scale demands server-centric, graph-aware source control. Code property graphs stop token bloat and prevent silent structural breakages. Versioning reasoning traces and execution histories alongside code keeps agents from repeating past mistakes. And stacked microdiffs offer a clean, isolated path for autonomous agents to ship code safely at scale.

item.title: Where Are the “Killer Apps” of AI?
item.dc:creator: Tim O’Reilly
item.description: Most of today’s AI entrepreneurs and social media enthusiasts are young. AI is the first technology revolution they’ve lived through. They don’t remember how unbelievably exciting it was in the late 1970s to get your own computer, instead of struggling to get time on one of the vast machines chugging away in what used to […]
item.content:encoded:
Most of today’s AI entrepreneurs and social media enthusiasts are young. AI is the first technology revolution they’ve lived through. They don’t remember how unbelievably exciting it was in the late 1970s to get your own computer, instead of struggling to get time on one of the vast machines chugging away in what used to be called “the glass house,” an air-conditioned room where from outside you could watch the nine-track tapes being accessed and the refrigerator-sized disk drives spinning. Input and output was on high-speed teletype printers (no screens) and magnetic tape (and before that on punch cards.) They also mostly don’t remember, as I do, writing assembly-language programs in which you moved data from one computer register to another, specified the arithmetic or logical operations to be performed on it, and then specified where to save the result.

They look at today’s AI and marvel at how virtually anyone can now generate code. They don’t realize that that’s also how it felt when you could use an interpreted programming language like BASIC to write your own applications instead of writing them in Assembler. They also don’t remember when Dan Bricklin used BASIC to write the first version of VisiCalc in 1979. He went into business with Bob Frankston, who rewrote it in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II. Dan was able to express the idea in Basic; Bob then wrote a tight, efficient version for widespread distribution. People rushed out to buy computers so they could use VisiCalc, and everyone predicted that the VisiCalc “spreadsheet” would put all the accountants out of work. It was the first program to be referred to as a “killer app.” It wasn’t the democratization of programming itself that was the killer app but what Dan and Bob did with it. In the entrepreneurial explosion that followed, databases, graphics, word processing, and other business applications came out of the glass house and, as Bill Gates put it, “onto every desk and into every home.”

We saw the same leap from astonishment to innovation to adoption with the World Wide Web. When O’Reilly demonstrated GNN, the first commercial website, to people at a trade show in 1993, attendees couldn’t believe that clicking on a link could pop up an image or a document from another computer thousands of miles away. They didn’t understand the difference between the software application (the web browser) from the network-connected documents with clickable hyperlinks that it acted as a frame for. They didn’t understand that web pages were a new kind of software written in a simple markup language anyone could understand. It didn’t make sense that the web page was a document that in many ways could look and act like a kind of program. And when people did understand, they thought that might be the end of programming.

In 1993, everyone thought that the web browser itself was the killer app, and that Marc Andreessen, the young creator of Mosaic, the most popular web browser, which became Netscape, was going to dethrone Bill Gates as the new king of computing. They didn’t realize that the true killer apps of the web were not the web browser and the web server but applications “up the stack” built using the new programming paradigm the web enabled. Those applications weren’t software as we’d known software before. They were database- and application-backed websites delivering services that were previously impossible. I remember thinking of Amazon as the 2005 equivalent to VisiCalc when a friend told me she had just bought her first computer so she could shop on Amazon. Once again, it wasn’t the new capability itself that was the killer app but what developers did with it.

What makes a killer app? I think that Tom Stoppard nailed it in his play Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead:

A man breaking his journey between one place and another at a third place of no name, character, population or significance, sees a unicorn cross his path and disappear. That in itself is startling, but there are precedents for mystical encounters of various kinds, or to be less extreme, a choice of persuasions to put it down to fancy; until—“My God,” says a second man, “I must be dreaming, I thought I saw a unicorn.” At which point, a dimension is added that makes the experience as alarming as it will ever be. A third witness, you understand, adds no further dimension but only spreads it thinner, and a fourth thinner still, and the more witnesses there are the thinner it gets and the more reasonable it becomes until it is as thin as reality, the name we give to the common experience.

That is, a killer app is at first a startling window onto an undreamed-of possibility, but one that so changes the paradigm that it rapidly gets taken for granted. In the meantime, everyone tries to make sense of the new world. Usually, their sensemaking is to try to reduce it to what they already know. The breakthrough entrepreneurs see more deeply and go farther.

In 1995 and 1996, almost everyone saw the future as a showdown between Microsoft and Netscape over who would own the web server and the web browser, and whether the web would supplant the desktop as the new platform. Microsoft won the browser wars, but it turned out to matter far less than anyone expected. The value went to the companies building on top of the browser, the ones that figured out what the network made possible.

The current narrative pitting AI model providers against each other sounds a lot like Microsoft versus Netscape to me. It is the platform war, the war for the layer that will become the common experience on which the revolutionary future will be built. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are the browsers of this era. That is not a small thing. But the browser wasn’t actually the killer app of the web. Netscape made money for a little while. Amazon and Google and the explosion of other sites were what made the web into something people couldn’t live without.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and the other coding agents may be the BASIC of this era, or like the tools and frameworks that made database-backed web applications possible. They are plumbing. Important plumbing, and plumbing that has to be in place before the future can truly happen. But still just plumbing. Inventors tend to spend decades maturing it, and O’Reilly tends to spend decades teaching people to build it. I suspect that will be just as true this time around.

In short, I’ve started asking myself whether we’ve actually seen the killer app for AI yet. The obvious assumption is that ChatGPT was. It certainly got a LOT of people excited and onboard very, very quickly. But maybe Claude Code was, enabling the breakthrough in agentic coding. Or maybe Hermes or Dots or Muse or some other personal agent will be. But we should take seriously the possibility that the killer app is not yet on the scene. These initial candidates for the killer app look too much like advances in a new enabling platform and not enough like a new generation of applications.

Personal agents may turn out to be a breakthrough category, but right now they look to me like early ecommerce before Amazon got it right.1 For Amazon to work, the web had to become secure enough for people to use credit cards online. The apps were waiting on missing mechanisms. For Google’s economic model to kick into gear, pay-per-click advertising had to be invented. I suspect we are in a similar moment waiting for crucial pieces to be dumped on the table so developers can complete their part of the puzzle. For AI agents to act on our behalf in the world, they will need their own equivalents: ways to pay, to prove who they are acting for, to be held accountable, and for the counterparties to settle on the allocation of the value created by the transaction. Ilan Strauss and I have argued in “The Missing Mechanisms of the Agentic Economy” that many of those mechanisms don’t exist yet. Maybe the killer apps are waiting on the equivalent of https and pay per click.

In short, when you listen to the AI conversation and mostly hear about people’s programming pipelines and how much more productive their programmers are, and very little about what they are using that productivity to build, you can be pretty confident that the killer apps haven’t arrived yet.

Where are we in the cycle?

Let’s line up the calendars and see if that tells us something useful.

CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers), the first widespread personal computer operating system, was developed in 1974, and the Altair 8800, the first mass-market personal computer, appeared on the cover of Popular Electronics in January 1975. Microsoft released a BASIC interpreter for it in June of that same year. A host of competing personal computer hardware platforms running CP/M were introduced soon thereafter. The Apple II was released in 1977, VisiCalc in October 1979, and dBase II in 1980. The IBM PC came out in August 1981 with Microsoft’s MS-DOS as its operating system. Lotus 1-2-3 (which included spreadsheet, graphing, and simple database features) was released in January 1983 and turned the PC into a business necessity.

In 1984, the revolutionary graphical user interface of the Macintosh was the next step function jump in the PC era. The GUI itself had been invented at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, but it wasn’t till Steve Jobs built his “insanely great” Mac that the world embraced it. Desktop publishing became the killer app of the GUI, with Aldus PageMaker and the Apple LaserWriter in 1985. The PC proper didn’t get the GUI till Windows 3.0 in 1990, but Microsoft’s embrace of it for applications such as Word (1983), Excel (1985), and PowerPoint (1987) as well as for the operating system and programming environment made it, for the time, master of the computing world.

So you can see a rough timeline. Four or five years from the introduction of the first version of what was to become the new platform to the first killer app. (Or two, if you count from the introduction of the Apple II, the platform for which VisiCalc was first written.) Then 10 years of invention, competition, and refinement, followed by fairly rapid consolidation and accumulation of market power.

Let’s do the same timeline for the web. Email and online forums might well have been the first internet killer apps, but they were really holdovers from previous generations of research networks. They were apps that had been evolving since the 1970s, though CompuServe and AOL had begun to bring them to the general public in the ’80s. The world really changed, though, when Tim Berners-Lee first wrote his proposal for what became the World Wide Web in March 1989. It was released to the world in August 1991. This was the new platform and the start of what would become the new programming paradigm.

Not too much happened outside physics labs and a few universities until 1993. (There were only about 200 websites when we published The Whole Internet User’s Guide and Catalog in November 1992.) In 1993, NCSA, the National Center for Supercomputer Applications, released Mosaic and we launched GNN, the first commercial website. Netscape shipped its browser, a follow-on to Mosaic, at the end of 1994. Yahoo! was launched that year too, Amazon, eBay, and the Altavista search engine in 1995, MapQuest in 1996, Google in 1998, and Wikipedia in 2001.

So, again about four years from the release of the platform to the appearance of the first killer app, and another 10 till the consolidation phase. (I see Gmail 2004, Google Maps 2005, Google Docs 2006, and Chrome 2008 as the equivalent of Microsoft’s release of Office on top of Windows as the beginning of the consolidation phase of the web.)

The timeline for mobile is not dissimilar. The iPhone in 2007, Android in 2008. Killer social apps Facebook and Twitter had gotten their start on the web at about the same time, but really came into their own on mobile over the next few years. The “could only have happened on mobile” killer apps of Uber, Lyft, and the on-demand economy didn’t arrive till 2011/2012.

A lot of people seem to think AI is moving way faster than previous technology revolutions. But if you line up the calendars, AI is moving at about the same pace as previous eras. Treat the transformer paper, “Attention Is All You Need,” published in June 2017, as the AI equivalent of Tim Berners-Lee’s 1989 proposal, and ChatGPT’s first release on November 30, 2022, as the equivalent of Mosaic. The gap from invention to breakout is about the same, five years for the web and five and a half for AI. That’s just getting the platform in place. The AI-native “killer apps” haven’t yet arrived but are due soon. (And please, let’s avoid the jokes that the “killer apps” of AI first showed up in the Russia-Ukraine drone war. That’s true, but not on the direct line of my argument here.)

On what seems to be a fairly consistent timeline, where are we today, then? October 2026 corresponds to roughly the spring of 1997. Amazon was about to go public. Hotmail was a year old. Google was still a research project at Stanford called BackRub. SixDegrees had kicked off social networking, but Facebook was still seven years off. Napster was still two years away.

Think of all those amazing application categories that had been pioneered, though. Search, ecommerce, email, and social networking were all in their infancy, but they were out there, delivering real value. I’m not sure that I see the equivalent time to value in AI. AI didn’t even get to Claude Code, its Microsoft Basic equivalent, till 2025! By some measures, AI is moving more slowly rather than more quickly. There’s more change to digest, and developers are still struggling with the tooling and developing the new knowledge that is needed.

Why so slow, with so much money?

The four largest hyperscalers are on track to spend roughly $700 billion in capital expenditure this year, nearly double what they spent in 2025. That is orders of magnitude more capital than went into the web in the 1990s. If capital and capability were the limiting factors, you’d think we should be well ahead of the earlier calendar, not behind.

I suspect that at least part of the answer is that Silicon Valley’s quest for premature monopoly may be making it less efficient at finding breakthroughs rather than more. Starting with the era of Uber and Lyft, massive VCs have canonized the winners at the beginning of the race, crowding out alternate technologies and business models. That may be happening here. But it’s also just in the nature of bubbles, which depend on groupthink to flourish.

And part of that groupthink is about where the value is going to be captured, rather than where it is going to be created. That is almost always backward looking. During the railroad boom, capital was pouring into building the tracks, and the new business models (think Montgomery Ward and Sears) that railroad enabled didn’t come till later. The dot-com bubble was far less capital intensive than people think. The telecom buildout that ran alongside it was where the money got spent. US carriers spent about $97 billion on capital in 2000 alone.

By 2002, according to an FDIC analysis, only 2% to 5% of the fiber in the ground was actually lit. More than 60 telecom companies went bankrupt. Once the data centers and dark fiber of the telecom bubble could be bought for pennies on the dollar, they enabled a generation of new applications like streaming video. YouTube was founded in 2005, after the crash, on cheap bandwidth that someone else had paid for before they went out of business. There were some visionary companies (think Google, Amazon) that had been started before the abundance arrived, but many more were founded after the bubble burst.

Carlota Perez’s book Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital documented this pattern across every technological revolution since the canal era. Financial capital pours into the installation of the new infrastructure, a bubble forms and bursts, and the deployment period that follows, when the technology actually reshapes the economy, is built by different people on top of what the crash left behind. If that is where we are in the cycle, then the absence of killer apps is not a puzzle at all.

The current data center buildout and the massive investments in frontier AI may not be the future. They are the infrastructure on which the future will be built. We have to ask ourselves what will we build once competition and overshoot and the bursting of the data center bubble make intelligence infrastructure cheap.

Help me fill in the picture

I see several possibilities. Either we are still early and the killer apps simply haven’t shown up yet, the way Google hadn’t shown up in 1997. Or AI is going more slowly than its boosters claim, in spite of all the capital, because capital and model capability are not the limiting factors. But it’s also possible that the killer apps are here, and I’m not hearing about them because the AI conversation is so focused on AI capability and nobody is telling the story of what they are accomplishing with it beyond building better developer tools.

I would like to know which. We all recognize a killer app when we see one. Amazon was a bookstore with more books than any physical bookstore could hold. Wikipedia was an encyclopedia written entirely by volunteers and was updated in real time within hours and sometimes even minutes of major events. Google Maps meant you always knew where you were and how to get anywhere else. If you know of an AI application, beyond the chatbot or agentic coding environment itself, that changes what ordinary people can do on that scale, or a business that does something an order of magnitude cheaper or better than the one it replaces, I want to hear about it. Tell me what you’re building in the Google Form below, and describe what tools you’re using only in the context of what they let you produce for others. If you’re a software developer using AI, what are you producing that was unthinkable before AI?

Tell me what you’re building

Footnote

  1. CommerceNet demonstrated the first encrypted credit card transaction online in 1994, and Netscape made the idea mainstream when it introduced HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) and made it available in the Netscape browser in that same year. This made it safe to type a credit card number onto a web page. ︎
